Q786001.summary: This bronze column, nearly four metres high, carries a relief band that spirals upward like the ancient columns of Trajan and Marcus Aurelius in Rome, but in place of imperial victories it shows the deeds of Christ. The lively figures follow his ministry from the Baptism in the Jordan to the Entry into Jerusalem. Commissioned by Bishop Bernward of Hildesheim, it once bore a triumphal cross at its summit, crowning the story of Christ's life with the sign of his victory.
facts: Bernward cast the column in conscious imitation of Trajan's Column and the Column of Marcus Aurelius; it is 3.79 m high and 58 cm in diameter.
The cross that crowned it was removed by iconoclasts in 1544 and melted down into a cannon; the present capital is a replacement made in 1870 by Karl Küsthardt.
Made for St. Michael's Church, it was moved to the cathedral precinct in 1810 and into the cathedral in 1893, returning there in 2014 after a temporary stay in St. Michael's.

cur:catacombs2-saint-maximin-innocents.summary: At the centre, between palm trees, a bearded Christ stands on the mountain of Paradise from which the four rivers flow, the Lamb at his side; he hands a book to Peter, who bows and carries a cross, and stretches his other hand to Paul. Around them Christ foretells Peter's denial (the cockerel perched between them) and gives him the keys, while Moses receives the Law and Abraham prepares to sacrifice Isaac at the ends. On the lid the shepherds adore the Christ Child warmed by the ox and ass, opposite Herod ordering the massacre of the Innocents.
facts: Long called the sarcophagus of Saint Maximin, it is now named after the Massacre of the Innocents on its lid; French Wikipedia describes the old name as mistaken.
The central Christ is bearded, unlike the youthful, beardless Christ of the miracle scenes, marking him as the exalted Lord giving the Law.
It is one of four late-4th-century sarcophagi in the crypt, which tradition associates with the burial of Mary Magdalene and her companions.
cur:catacombs2-saint-maximin-innocents.original_title: Sarcophage du massacre des saints Innocents (dit de saint Maximin)

cur:manuscripts-egberti-feeding-multitud.summary: Christ stands frontally at the centre between two apostles, labelled 'apostoli', receiving and blessing the loaves and fishes, while the seated crowd, labelled 'turbae', fills both sides of the picture.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
During the Second World War the codex was evacuated to Giessen University Library, survived its bombing in December 1944, and was brought back to Trier in May 1945 from a parsonage at Elkerhausen.

cur:objects-berlin-forty-martyrs-ivory.summary: Forty naked soldiers huddle and writhe on the frozen lake of Sebaste, where they were condemned to die of cold for their faith; one turns away toward the warm bath-house at the right. Above them Christ sits enthroned in heaven between angels holding crowns, ready to reward their endurance. The plaque is a masterpiece of Byzantine figure carving, contrasting suffering below with the calm glory of Christ above.
facts: The museum records that the plaque (inv. 574) was acquired in 1828 from the Bartoldi collection.

According to the traditional accounts, the Forty Martyrs were soldiers of the Legio XII Fulminata martyred near Sebaste in Lesser Armenia in 320; the earliest account is a homily of Basil of Caesarea (Wikipedia).
